results.authorRaw:
The market stall’s canvas roof snapped in the wind off the Ascendant Run, and Carys’s hand hovered above the folded note I still held between my fingers. I could not make myself release it. The youth’s binding still flickered in my mind, the elder’s demand still pressed at the back of my throat, and every breath I took tasted of the spiralgrass crushed underfoot.

Carys leaned closer, her voice low so the other vendors would not hear. “If you keep it any longer the ink will smudge from your sweat. Give it over.”

My thumb traced the edge of the parchment once more. The note carried the only proof we had that the bloodline geas had been tampered with before the youth ever stepped into the circle. Handing it across meant someone else would know what Julian had already risked to shield us both.

I let the paper slide from my palm. Carys took it without flourish, tucking it beneath a bolt of dyed river-silk as though it were nothing more than a price list. Her eyes flicked up once, sharp, then away.

Behind us the crowd thickened at the next stall. A voice rose above the rest—clear, carrying, the sort that belonged to someone used to being listened to. The council messenger who had arrived at the clearing was reading from a sealed letter, the one that had been intercepted with the token from Julian’s house. The words carried across the market air.

“…three wishes offered in the old manner, each bound to the same bloodline, each paid for in secret. The first for safety of the line, the second for the return of what was lost, the third—”

The rest was lost beneath the sudden rush of voices. People turned. Some laughed, thinking it theater. Others went still, because the old manner meant sacrifice that could not be undone. I felt the weight of every eye that might turn next toward me.

Carys’s fingers tightened on the silk. “They will trace it back,” she said. “You need to decide which one you can afford to unmake.”

The choice sat between us like a live coal. The first wish had kept the line from fracturing when my father left. The second had brought back a fragment of what the Becoming had taken from Julian. Either one undone would cost more than either of us had left to give.

I realized that old tarot deck is still in my hand. Reassuringly solid. Present. One of the heavy gold cards slips out — "Petition Fate" is inscribed in it. If only it were that easy. I would wish myself a way out. No — a way in. If only…

The canvas roof of the stall snapped again, the wind off the Ascendant Run whipping the edges like a living thing. I kept my fingers pressed against the folded note in my pocket, the binding’s glow still needling at my skin. The gatekeeper—his perpetually squinting eyes refused to meet mine—stood with his arms crossed, the silver rings on his fingers catching the dull light as he shifted his weight from heel to toe. The vendors’ shouts blurred together into a wall of sound, but his silence was louder.

“You don’t get to look away,” I said, stepping closer until the hem of my skirt brushed the edge of his boot. The determination in my stance was a weight I carried like a second heartbeat, the gold cap of my tooth catching the light as I pressed my lips together. “Which road did he take?”

His gaze flickered toward the eastern edge of the square, where the road split like a forked tongue against the horizon. The hesitation in his shoulders was a language I knew well—every second he delayed was another day she didn’t come home. “There are three,” he muttered, voice rough as gravel underfoot. “But only one leads where you think it does.”

I leaned in, the scent of sandalwood and sweat clinging to him. “Don’t play games. I can feel the wish still humming in my bones. Tell me.”

His fingers twitched toward the knife at his belt, but he didn’t draw it. “The middle one. The one with the cracked stones. But it’s not just the road, girl. It’s what’s at the end of it.” His voice dropped, the words like a blade pressed against my ribs. “You really want to see?”

The vendors’ shouts blurred together into a wall of sound, but they thinned around the space he left empty.“You don’t get to look away,” I said, stepping closer until the hem of my skirt brushed the edge of his boot. The determination settled in my stance before I could loosen it, my tongue tapping once against the gold cap of my tooth as I pressed my lips together.“Which road did he take?”His gaze flickered toward the eastern edge of the square, where the road split against the horizon. His shoulders carried a hesitation I recognized—every second he delayed was another day she didn’t come home.“There are three,” he muttered, his voice catching on the last word.“But only one leads where you think it does.”I leaned in, the scent of sandalwood and sweat clinging to him.“Don’t play games. I can feel the wish still humming in my bones. Tell me.”His fingers twitched toward the knife at his belt, but he didn’t draw it.“The middle one. The one with the cracked stones. But it’s not just the road, girl. It’s what’s at the end of it.”His voice dropped, the words drawing the space between us narrower.“You really want to see?”“Tempt Fate.”Grandma never let me play with that one. A sword raised to a blood-red sky, lightning arcing down from the clouds (or maybe arcing up?) Ow! results.authorRaw:
The canvas roof of the stall snapped again, the wind off the Ascendant Run drawing the edges outward in sharp tugs. I kept my fingers pressed against the folded note in my pocket, the binding’s glow still needling at my skin. The gatekeeper—his perpetually squinting eyes refused to meet mine—stood with his arms crossed, the silver rings on his fingers clicking once as he shifted his weight from heel to toe.

The brazier’s iron basin glowed at my hip, its heat seeping through the cloth of my coat like a warning. I could feel the weight of the letters, thick and uneven in their envelope, the sigils along the seals still humming faintly against my thigh. The gatekeeper’s gaze flicked toward the envelope, then back to the rents in the canvas above, as if he could will the wind to tear the stall apart entirely and spare him from having to speak.

Carys stepped forward, her boots scuffing against the packed dirt, her expression unreadable. "You really want to see?" Her voice was low, pitched just for me, the words carrying the same weight they had in the market when she’d first pressed the note into my hands. The same weight as the binding that had coiled around my wrist when I’d touched the envelope, the same weight as the look in her eyes when she’d said, "Read it aloud. Let Fate decide."

I didn’t answer. The gatekeeper’s fingers tightened around his own ring, the metal biting into his palm. The brazier’s light caught the silver in his rings, sending a flicker across the stall’s shadows, turning the silver momentarily into something like eyes watching me. The air smelled of iron and old wood, of the river’s damp and the smoke from the brazier that never quite went out.

The gatekeeper exhaled through his nose, a sound like a sigh turned into a curse. "You know what happens if you burn something bound to Fate." His voice was rough, the kind of voice that had carried orders across battlefields and through council chambers. "The fire burns back."

I pulled the letter free, the envelope stiff against my fingers. The sigils pulsed once, a slow breath of light, as if the paper itself was alive and knew what I was about to do. Carys’s breath hitched, just barely, but she didn’t reach for me. She just watched, her hands clenched at her sides, the same way she’d watched me take the relic from the shrine table. Like she was waiting for me to do something irreversible.

The gatekeeper’s eyes finally met mine, and there was something in them I hadn’t seen before—something like fear, or maybe recognition. "You understand the cost," he said. It wasn’t a question.

I did. I understood the cost of keeping them. I understood the cost of burning them.

The brazier’s heat licked at my back, the iron basin radiating like a heartbeat against my spine. I held the letter over the flames, the sigils flaring brighter as they neared the heat. The gatekeeper didn’t move. Carys didn’t breathe. The wind outside the stall howled, the canvas groaning as if it, too, was holding its breath.

I hesitated. The letter was warm in my hands, the paper softening at the edges where the sigils bled into the fibers. The gatekeeper’s rings clicked again, a sound like a countdown. Carys’s gaze was fixed on the letter, her lips parted slightly, her fingers twitching toward the hilt of the knife at her belt.

I lowered the letter, just a fraction. The sigils dimmed, as if disappointed.

The gatekeeper’s shoulders sagged, just barely. "Then you understand the cost of keeping them."

I exhaled, slow and deliberate. The letter’s heat against my fingers was like a pulse, like the thrum of a spell that had already taken root. I looked at Carys, her face half-lit by the brazier’s glow, her eyes reflecting the flames like embers. She looked at me like she was waiting for an answer I wasn’t ready to give.

The wind outside howled again, the stall shuddering as if it, too, was waiting.

I lifted the letter higher, the sigils flaring once more, a last defiance before the flames claimed them. The gatekeeper’s breath caught. Carys’s hands tightened around the knife.

I let the letter fall.
